MIL §4.2 concludes with a proof of Cantor's theorem, which I have refactored as follows:

import Mathlib.Data.Set.Function

variable {α : Type*}
open Function

theorem Cantor : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f surjf
  let X := { a | a ∉ f a }
  obtain ⟨x, fx_eq_X⟩ := surjf X
  by_cases h : x ∈ X
  repeat -- The same reasoning applies whether x ∈ X or x ∉ X
    let h' := h        -- In the spirit of Forth's `dup`
    simp [X] at h'     -- We do our rewriting in the _copy_ h'
    rw [fx_eq_X] at h' -- After this rewrite, h' = ¬h
    contradiction

What I especially like about the above is how repeat reveals the same reasoning applies to each of the by_cases. To make this clear, here's my handwritten proof for comparison:

  1. Assume f:S→2Sf : S \rightarrow 2^Sf:S→2S is surjective.
  2. Let X={a∈S∣a∉f(a)}X = \{a \in S \mid a \notin f(a)\}X={a∈S∣a∈/f(a)}.
  3. X∈2S  ⟹  ∃x such that f(x)=XX \in 2^S \implies \exists x \text{ such that } f(x) = XX∈2S⟹∃x such that f(x)=X
  4. Now either x∈Xx\in Xx∈X or x∉Xx\notin Xx∈/X:
    (a) x∈X  ⟹  x∉f(x)  ⟹  x∉X→←x \in X \implies x \notin f(x) \implies x \notin X \quad \rightarrow\leftarrowx∈X⟹x∈/f(x)⟹x∈/X→←
    (b) x∉X  ⟹  x∈f(x)  ⟹  x∈X→←x \notin X \implies x \in f(x) \implies x \in X \quad \rightarrow\leftarrowx∈/X⟹x∈f(x)⟹x∈X→←

My question is about the let h' := h, which somehow feels inelegant (even non-functional) to me. Is there a tactic (or other standard idiom) for this kind of thing in Lean — duplicating a hypothesis so that you can rewrite it while retaining the original?
what's wrong with simply have h' := h?

You can sort-of use absurd:

import Mathlib.Data.Set.Function
example {α} : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬f.Surjective := by
  intro f surjf
  let X := { a | a ∉ f a }
  have ⟨x, fx_eq_X⟩ := surjf X
  by_cases h : x ∈ X
  all_goals
    absurd h
    try dsimp [X]
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    assumption

I see that works equally well. I've been tending to use have when I want to spell out explicitly a hypothesis that would otherwise be obscure. Here, however, let seems (judging from the name alone, as a Lean newbie) to express my intent better. I guess what I'm aiming at is a 'higher level' expression of this intent, perhaps one that announces a plan to transform h' to contradict h.

Thanks, @Snir Broshi! I can see that absurd works very nicely here, and eliminates the need to copy h. Now I have the following:

theorem Cantor : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f surjf
  let X := { a | a ∉ f a }
  obtain ⟨x, fx_eq_X⟩ := surjf X
  by_cases h : x ∈ X
  all_goals
    absurd h
    dsimp [X]
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    exact h

Also, it seems all_goals better expresses the fact I was pointing to with repeat.
You can also use <;>

Usually, the let/have distinction is about propositions versus "data". If you have a proposition, use have. If you e.g. define a map, use let. (For instance, X above is using let and now have.) This is a rule of thumb, so there are (few) exceptions --- but it will get you very far.

Ruben Van de Velde said:

You can also use <;>

Replacing all_goals verbatim by <;> didn't work; how did you mean to use <;>?

by_cases h : x ∈ X <;>
  · absurd h
    dsimp [X]
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    exact h

or

  by_cases h : x ∈ X <;> (absurd h; dsimp [X]; rw [fx_eq_X]; exact h)

or

  by_cases h : x ∈ X <;> {
    absurd h
    dsimp [X]
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    exact h
  }

With above suggestions, my current refactoring would be:

import Mathlib.Data.Set.Function

variable {α : Type*}
open Function

theorem Cantor : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f surjf
  let X := { a | a ∉ f a }
  obtain ⟨x, fx_eq_X⟩ := surjf X
  by_cases h : x ∈ X
  all_goals
    dsimp [X] at h
    absurd h
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    exact h

I can now step through this proof and watch an exact recapitulation of my manual proof. Doing dsimp [X] at h before absurd seems necessary for preserving 'parallel structure', since

  • absurd (h : x ∈ X) yields ⊢ x ∈ f x whereas
  • absurd (h : ¬x ∈ X) yields ⊢ x ∈ X.

Jeremy Chen said:

  by_cases h : x ∈ X <;>
  · absurd h
    dsimp [X]
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    exact h

or

  by_cases h : x ∈ X <;> (absurd h; dsimp [X]; rw [fx_eq_X]; exact h)

I like these very much, especially maybe the first. The editor indicated scoping was an issue, and I had tried tossing in some braces but perhaps didn't take sufficient care with indentation. (Incidentally, I can see now that the . plays a role w.r.t. scoping something like that in Principia Mathematica?)

Using

by_cases h : x ∈ X <;>
· dsimp [X] at h
  absurd h
  rw [fx_eq_X]
  assumption

confers the additional advantage that the original h gets retained as h✝ even after the dsimp [X] at h.

constructive proof:

theorem Cantor : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f hf
  have ⟨x, hfx⟩ := hf { x | x ∉ f x }
  have h : (x ∈ f x) = (x ∉ f x) := congrArg (x ∈ ·) hfx
  simp at h
Maybe you like the (a)symmetry here more, idk
Or if you like automation, by_cases x ∈ X <;> grind will close your original proof

Jeremy Chen said:

constructive proof:

theorem Cantor : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f hf
  have ⟨x, hfx⟩ := hf { x | x ∉ f x }
  have h : (x ∈ f x) = (x ∉ f x) := congrArg (x ∈ ·) hfx
  simp at h

That's TBH the kind of proof that I found so "inscrutable" in Agda. (No doubt, I'll be able to revisit Agda sometime in future, after the more gentle introduction I'm finding through Lean.)

For this proof, I do rather like setting forth X explicitly as the 'problematical' construction that engenders all the subsequent mayhem. The X object makes for a handy conceptual focus. (Compare the Russell paradox, with its own problematical set construction.)

My now-preferred proof is as follows:

theorem Cantor : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f surjf
  let X := { a | a ∉ f a }
  obtain ⟨x, fx_eq_X⟩ := surjf X
  by_cases h : x ∈ X <;>
  · dsimp [X] at h
    absurd h
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    assumption

Is this somehow not constructive? (Or 'less' constructive?)
the part where you by_cases h : x ∈ X is less constructive because it uses excluded middle

This has really taught me something. It begins to look now as if

  have h : (x ∈ f x) = (x ∉ f x)

constitutes the essential core of the proof, which my by_cases danced around with a superfluous appeal to EM.

not-not-em is constructive though, so you can use that instead

theorem Cantor : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f surjf
  let X := { a | a ∉ f a }
  obtain ⟨x, fx_eq_X⟩ := surjf X
  refine not_not_em (x ∈ X) fun em => ?_
  rcases em with h | h <;>
  · dsimp [X] at h
    absurd h
    rw [fx_eq_X]
    assumption
Tangent: cantor's theorem is an instance of Lawvere's fixed point theorem, which is valid in any cartesian closed category, hence we should expect it to be constructively true

you might be interested in Lawvere’s fixpoint theorem, which states that the existence of a surjective function $f: A \to B^A$ means that every function $g: B \to B$ has a fixed point — the “essential core” you refer to above states that the proposition (x ∈ f x) is a fixed point of Not: Prop -> Prop, which is a contradiction.

ah! you beat me by a few seconds :)) there’s also a lean presentation of this fact linked here: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/187764-Lean-for-teaching/topic/accidentally.20deleted.20my.20game.20from.20the.20Lean.20game.20server/near/593249225

Ha, looking back at my notebook for Egbert Rijke's Intro to Homotopy Type Theory, I see the very last problem I worked was 4.3(b) — and 4.3(c)(iv) is precisely to show ¬¬(P+¬P)\neg\neg(P + \neg P)¬¬(P+¬P). Probably time to get back to that! :sweat_smile:

Edit: but maybe more to the point is 4.3(a)(ii) ¬(P↔¬P)\neg(P\leftrightarrow\neg P)¬(P↔¬P)? Isn't that precisely the shape of

have h : (x ∈ f x) = (x ∉ f x)

?

Thomas Waring said:

there’s also a lean presentation of this fact linked here

Also docs#Function.exists_fixed_point_of_surjective

The more I looked at

  have h : (x ∈ f x) = (x ∉ f x) := congrArg (x ∈ ·) hfx

the more it looked like :fire: :fire: :fire: .

But it seems to me that the explicit typing here conceals a transformation I'd rather make explicit. So FWIW my own preferred proof might now be:

theorem Cantor''' : ∀ f : α → Set α, ¬Surjective f := by
  intro f surjf
  let X := { x | x ∉ f x }    -- introduce the [problematical] set construction ..
  have ⟨x, fx_eq_X⟩ := surjf X -- incidentally allowing helpful _naming_ of (f x = X)
  have k : (x ∈ f x) = (x ∈ X) := congrArg (x ∈ ·) fx_eq_X -- congrArg _verbatim_
  simp [X] at k -- eliminate the X introduced above .. et voilà! [and/or bwahahah]
